# A failed LLM call is invisible in `$REBAR_USAGE_LOG`

## Reported by

`rebar review-code` on change 1178 (story b690), as a medium/correctness advisory finding against that change. **Verified and confirmed PRE-EXISTING, not introduced by b690** — b690 only added `step`/`model_class` fields to rows that are written; the omission of failed calls predates it.

## Mechanism (verified by reading the control flow, not inferred)

`PydanticAIRunner.run()` calls `usage_log.record(...)` at the END of the method, AFTER the `try/except` whose except spine is `interpret_failure(exc, ...)`, and `interpret_failure` ALWAYS re-raises. So when a model call raises — budget exceeded, provider error, unretryable output, sampling error — control leaves `run()` without ever reaching `record()`, and NO usage row is written for a call that may have burned substantial input tokens.

## What this does and does not cost

**Failure spend is not lost entirely.** `usage_log.failure_usage()` builds safe counters (requests, tool_calls, the four token fields, finish_reason) and `structured_run.py` attaches them as `exc.diagnostic` at four sites (`:91`, `:100`, `:119`, `:134`), which reach the durable gate-error sidecar. So the information exists.

**But it never reaches the usage log**, which means:
- a spend total folded from the JSONL by `summarize()` UNDER-REPORTS actual spend, silently, by
  exactly the failed calls. That summary is what the two billable weekly CI jobs
  (`external-integration.yml`, `prompt-eval.yml`) publish to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`.
- the per-step attribution added by b690 cannot see failed calls, so "which pass is expensive?"
  is answerable only for calls that succeeded — and a retry-to-exhaustion failure is precisely the
  expensive case an operator would want attributed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] a failed LLM call writes a usage row carrying the same identifying fields a successful one
      does (`op`, `step`, `model_class`, `model`, `provider`) plus whatever token counters are
      known, so a JSONL spend total includes failed calls
- [ ] the row is distinguishable from a successful call (so a reader can separate delivered work
      from burned budget) — the shape is the implementer's call, but it must be explicit, not
      inferred from a missing field
- [ ] asserted by a test in which the model RAISES and the log is then read — not by reading
      `usage_log.py`, and not by asserting on `failure_usage()` in isolation, since the defect is
      about what reaches the FILE
- [ ] the existing no-op-when-unset and `summarize()`-still-folds guarantees still hold
- [ ] telemetry must never break the call path: the record must not convert a provider failure into
      a different exception, nor swallow the original (the existing `record()` already swallows its
      own OSError for this reason — preserve that discipline)
- [ ] no double-counting: a call that fails and is then RETRIED must not be recorded such that the
      same spend appears twice as delivered work

## Note on scope

Not fixed inside b690 deliberately: b690's change is a one-line model-resolution fix plus its observability prerequisite, and moving `record()` across an exception boundary is a distinct behavioural change to the failure path with its own double-counting and never-break-the-call-path risks. Filed under epic 061c because the usage log is that epic's measurement instrument.
baseline.summary: Usage log omits failed LLM calls: record() sits after run()'s except spine, so a raising call writes no row

baseline.description:
# The bugfix-size attestation gate is unsatisfiable for any locally-reviewed bug

## Context / Problem

`bugfix_size_gate.py` (landed on main 2026-08-03, commit 1920dc9fe5) BLOCKS a Gerrit change whose `rebar-ticket:` bug carries >150 non-test changed lines unless that bug has an acceptable plan-review attestation. Its "cross-host verification" design constraint is explicit:

    the review bot is NOT the environment that signed the attestation, so this module verifies
    the op-cert against the PINNED `.rebar/trusted_environments.yaml` keyring (never the bot's
    own env key), mirroring `verify_required_environment`'s not-pinned arm for unpinned
    principals.

`.rebar/trusted_environments.yaml` pinned exactly ONE environment when this ticket was filed: `9f1c8e42-7a3b-4d5e-b6c1-2f0a9d8e7c65` (`nava-opcert-prod`), whose private half "lives ONLY in SSM /rebar/prod/opcert-ed25519-key".

> **Correction, as of the reviewed tree.** That file now pins **TWO** environments: Gerrit 1355
> (merged, `75cdfec357`) added `ade0f2ef-51cc-45a2-bb97-c09846cd3df5`, this maintainer's own gate
> environment, and that is the principal which signed `129e`'s attestation. The paragraphs below
> describe the pre-1355 state and are kept as the ticket's history. The pin resolved the blockage
> for ONE machine and is precisely why this ticket stayed open: it did not make the criterion
> satisfiable for anyone else, and pinning is CODEOWNERS-gated so a contributor cannot self-serve
> it.

A plan review run by a developer signs with that developer's own env id as the DSSE principal. That principal is not pinned, so `trusted_env_keyring(principal, repo_root)` returns None and the gate takes its not-pinned arm:

    {"verdict": "mismatch",
     "reason": "signing environment '<env>' is not pinned in trusted_environments.yaml"}

which is an affirmative invalid classification, so it BLOCKS (it is not one of the fail-open infrastructure arms, and it is not one of the ACCEPTED `stale-code`/`stale-head` drift arms).

**So a large bug fix can only clear this gate with an attestation produced by the prod op-cert environment — and there is no way to obtain one.** The deployed `opcert` service does accept `{"ticket_id", "kind": "plan-review"}` on `POST /opcert/jobs` and signs with the SSM key, but:

1. **no client exists in the repo.** `grep` for `opcert/jobs` outside `opcert_service/app.py`
   finds only the nginx template, the terraform output description, and unit tests. Callers are
   expected to SigV4-sign to an API Gateway endpoint; nothing in `rebar` does.
2. **the service deliberately cannot persist what it signs.** compose sets
   `REBAR_SYNC_PUSH: "off"` with the comment "a gate's SIGNATURE append lands only in the
   discarded per-job workspace". It returns the `envelope` in the job record, and there is no
   rebar CLI that records a returned envelope onto a ticket as its attestation.
3. **the guard is a production secret.** `/opcert/jobs` fails closed without the
   `X-Opcert-Guard` header, materialized from SSM `/rebar/prod/opcert-origin-guard`.

## Evidence this is live, not theoretical

Gerrit change 1344 (bug `129e-2d88-cce2-492c`, 554 non-test lines) is **`Verified +1`** with its only blocking finding being this criterion. Its plan review PASSED and was re-signed locally; the gate's complaint moved from "unsigned; no plan-review attestation record" (patchset 1) to "mismatch; signing environment 'ade0f2ef-…' is not pinned" (patchset 2), i.e. the signature IS seen and is rejected solely on provenance. No code finding blocks the change.

`129e` in turn `blocks` epic `061c-ecd1-8967-4a76`, so this gate currently blocks an epic.

## Why no existing bug fix hit this first

The gate landed 2026-08-03. The only recent bug fix over the floor, `e3cd-ba36-41c3-4661` (229 non-test lines), merged 2026-08-02 — ONE DAY BEFORE the gate existed — and carries no attestation at all (`review-plan --status` -> "unsigned"). So there is no precedent path; 129e appears to be the first change to actually meet this gate.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/llm/code_review/bugfix_size_gate.py` — the not-pinned arm's severity/classification.
- `.rebar/trusted_environments.yaml` — whether developer signing environments are pinnable at all.
- a missing client for the op-cert service (submit + record the returned envelope), if the
  intended answer is that large bug fixes must be prod-attested.
- `docs/plan-review-gate.md` / the packaged code-review guide — neither tells an author how to
  obtain an acceptable attestation for a large fix.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] a large bug fix authored in a developer environment has a DOCUMENTED, EXECUTABLE path to an
      attestation this gate accepts — demonstrated end to end on a real change, not by inspection
- [x] the not-pinned arm's behaviour is a deliberate, recorded decision: either it stays blocking
      and the path above exists, or it is reclassified (e.g. advisory when NO developer environment
      is pinnable), with the security reasoning written down
- [x] the failure message names the remedy, so an author hitting it is not left to reverse-engineer
      trusted_environments.yaml and the compose file to discover why a PASSING plan review is
      rejected
- [x] the gate still requires a genuine, PASSED, signed plan-review attestation BOUND TO THIS
      ticket and kind, so an unreviewed change cannot self-certify. RESTATED under the operator's
      design decision (see "Security reasoning" below): trust now rests on the FACT of a completed
      attested review, NOT on the signing environment's provenance. The original wording
      ("does NOT let a change self-certify from an untrusted environment") described the
      provenance-gated design that this ticket exists to retire, and is superseded.

## Fix plan (operator's design decision — implemented as current policy, not a config framework)

The attestation check must NOT gate on the SOURCE of certification. It gates ONLY on the FACT that an attested plan review has been completed, plus that attestation's lifecycle/freshness validity.

1. `src/rebar/llm/code_review/bugfix_size_gate.py` — delete the cross-host source-of-certification
   chain: the `trusted_env_keyring` lookup + not-pinned `mismatch` arm, the `verify_opcert` call,
   and `_plan_review_anchor` (whose only consumer was `verify_opcert`'s era anchoring). The verdict
   vocabulary shrinks to the `compute_validity` literals plus the gate's own `error`; unknown
   literals still fail OPEN (infra/advisory).

   **`verify_opcert` also carried the subject binding (its Phase 0), so deleting it would drop
   that too — therefore the binding is RE-ASSERTED IN THIS MODULE, explicitly, as its own step.**
   `verify_opcert` was the only site enforcing it; nothing downstream replaces it
   (`opcert_from_record` merely decodes, and `compute_validity` verifies no signature and checks no
   ticket id). The new chain is four steps, not three:

   1. attestation record present, else `unsigned`;
   2. decodable op-cert envelope, else `unsigned`;
   3. **subject binding, read from the SIGNED payload's predicate** (`bound["ticket_id"]` and
      `bound["kind"]`, never the record's plaintext mirror): a cert minted for a different ticket,
      or of a different kind, returns `wrong-kind` -> FLAG -> BLOCK. This is kept because it asks
      WHAT the attestation covers, not WHO signed it, so it is orthogonal to the provenance
      question this ticket retires — and it is what stops a valid cert being replayed off another
      ticket;
   4. `compute_validity` lifecycle/freshness (`stale-material`, `stale-reopened`, phase, pins).

   What is NOT retained, stated without euphemism: step 3 reads the signed payload but nothing
   re-checks the DSSE signature, because with no pinned key there is no trust root to check it
   against. See "Security reasoning" for why that is the deliberate choice and what it costs.
2. `tests/unit/test_bugfix_size_gate_ad0d.py` — RED oracle: invert
   `test_classify_unpinned_foreign_environment_flags` into
   `test_classify_unpinned_foreign_environment_is_accepted`, and realign the vocabulary tests.
3. `docs/plan-review-gate.md` — new section documenting the Gerrit bugfix-size attestation gate
   and its executable remedy (AC1).
4. `src/rebar/_guides/passing-code-review.md` — the author-facing on-ramp for the same (AC1).
5. AC3 is satisfied by removal: the message that named no remedy is gone, and the only remaining
   blocking finding is the teaching finding, which names `rebar review-plan <id>`.

Explicitly out of scope, and deliberately so: no op-cert service client, no configurable trust-policy framework. This is the current policy, "for now".

## Testing

RED-first. The proving oracle is `tests/unit/test_bugfix_size_gate_ad0d.py::test_classify_unpinned_signing_environment_is_accepted` plus `::test_oversized_bug_fix_reviewed_in_an_unpinned_environment_does_not_block`, both of which mint a genuinely signed plan-review op-cert from an unpinned principal in a fixture store with no `.rebar/trusted_environments.yaml` at all. Both were observed FAILING on `main` with `verdict == 'mismatch'` / `'BLOCK'` before the fix existed, and were held out from the implementer.

- `pytest tests/unit/test_bugfix_size_gate_ad0d.py -q` — 37 passed (was 35 + 2 red).
- `pytest tests/unit/test_review_bot_retrigger_attestation_6a81.py -q` — 15 passed; the
  `recheck-review` re-check stays fail-closed on every non-accepted bucket.
- Mutation check: re-inserting the exact root cause (the `trusted_env_keyring(...) is None ->
  mismatch` arm) returns both oracles to RED; restoring the fix returns them to GREEN.
- `pytest tests/unit -q` — 4313 passed, 9 skipped.
- Subject-binding regressions (added on plan-review feedback):
  `test_classify_rejects_a_cert_bound_to_another_ticket` and
  `test_classify_rejects_a_cert_of_another_kind` — both must classify `wrong-kind` (BLOCK).
- Replication on the REAL reported change, not a fixture (AC1): with
  `.rebar/trusted_environments.yaml` DELETED — the exact condition in the report, no developer
  environment pinnable at all — `classify_plan_review_attestation('129e-2d88-cce2-492c')` returns
  `stale-head` -> bucket `accepted`. Before the fix the identical call returned
  `mismatch` ("signing environment 'ade0f2ef-…' is not pinned") -> bucket `flag` -> BLOCK.
  That is Gerrit 1344's blocking finding, gone, without the pin.
- `make lint` and `make typecheck` — both clean (mypy: 432 files, no issues).


## Security reasoning (AC2 — the deliberate, recorded decision)

**What was removed and why there is no middle path.** The old chain verified the DSSE signature via `verify_opcert` against the keyring `trusted_env_keyring(principal)` returns — i.e. against `.rebar/trusted_environments.yaml`. That file IS the trust root. When the principal is not pinned there is NO key to verify against, so "keep signature verification but relax only the not-pinned arm" is not actually a posture: an attacker simply signs with an unpinned principal and takes the relaxed arm. The two coherent options are (a) every accepted attestation must be signed by a pinned key — which is unsatisfiable for any contributor, since pinning is CODEOWNERS-gated on the code branch and no contributor can add themselves; and (b) accept the FACT of a recorded, well-formed, subject-bound, lifecycle-valid plan-review attestation. The operator chose (b), for now.

**What that costs, stated plainly.** The attestation record lives on the auto-pushed, non-Gerrit- gated tickets branch, which `opcert.opcert_from_record` documents as attacker-writable. Under (b) this criterion is therefore an ANTI-SLOPPINESS gate ("did you actually write and review a plan before shipping 150+ non-test lines under a bug label?"), not an ANTI-ADVERSARY one. Anyone able to write the tickets branch can fabricate a record that satisfies it.

**Why that is acceptable here.** This gate was never the adversarial boundary. Landing on `main` still requires `LLM-Review +1` AND `Verified +1`, both cast only by bots/admins, plus no unresolved comments — so a fabricated attestation buys an attacker nothing except the removal of one coaching block. The code branch itself remains Gerrit-gated and CODEOWNERS-protected, which is where the pin file and the review rubric live. Nothing in this change widens who may vote.

**What is retained.** Subject binding is kept — re-implemented as an explicit step in `classify_plan_review_attestation` because `verify_opcert` was its only previous home (see Fix plan step 1.3) — because it asks WHAT the attestation covers rather than WHO signed it: a cert bound to another ticket, or of another kind, classifies `wrong-kind` and BLOCKS (regressions `test_classify_rejects_a_cert_bound_to_another_ticket`, `test_classify_rejects_a_cert_of_another_kind`, the latter proving the lying plaintext mirror is ignored in favour of the signed payload). Lifecycle and freshness are untouched: `stale-material` still blocks, so attest-then-edit-the-plan is still not a bypass. A missing attestation is still `unsigned` -> BLOCK, which is the gate's whole point. Unknown verdicts still fail OPEN, so the removal can never become a surprise block.

**Why not the pinning alternative (Gerrit 1355, already merged).** Pinning env `ade0f2ef-…` fixed the blockage for ONE maintainer's machine while leaving the criterion unsatisfiable for everyone else — it is the reason this ticket stayed open after that change landed. Scaling it means pinning every contributor's environment in a CODEOWNERS-gated file, i.e. an admin round-trip before anyone can land a large bug fix, and a growing keyring whose entries are never revoked. That trades a real, recurring delivery block for a security property this gate does not actually provide (see "What that costs"). The pin stays in place and still verifies where it applies; it is simply no longer load-bearing for this criterion.

**Reversibility.** "For now" is not a promise of a mechanism. Restoring provenance gating is re-adding the keyring lookup + `verify_opcert` call to `classify_plan_review_attestation`; the `ACCEPTED`/`FLAG`/`INFRA` partition and the fail-open default are unchanged, so nothing else has to move. No config key, flag, or policy framework is introduced — deliberately, since a switch nobody can flip safely is worse than an explicit, documented policy.

## Affected consumers (beyond the edited files)

`src/rebar/review_bot/retrigger.py` is not edited but its behaviour changes by design: it reuses this module's `classify_plan_review_attestation` + `bucket_for_verdict` for the self-service `recheck-review` precondition, so an attestation from an unpinned developer environment now unlocks a re-review where it previously refused. That is the intended outcome (it is the same unsatisfiability bug seen from the retrigger side) and it stays FAIL-CLOSED: any bucket other than `accepted` still refuses. Covered by `tests/unit/test_review_bot_retrigger_attestation_6a81.py` (15 passed).
baseline.summary: bugfix-size attestation gate is unsatisfiable for any locally-reviewed bug — only the prod op-cert env is pinned and it has no client

baseline.description:
## Context / Problem

The `commit-msg` hook install command documented in AGENTS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md is WORKTREE-UNSAFE. It silently clobbers the shared, pre-commit-managed hook for EVERY worktree, and the damage is invisible until a Gerrit push is rejected for a missing `Change-Id`.

The documented command:

    curl -sLo "$(git rev-parse --git-path hooks/commit-msg)" https://rebar.solutions.navateam.com/tools/hooks/commit-msg && chmod +x "$(git rev-parse --git-path hooks/commit-msg)"

`git rev-parse --git-path hooks/commit-msg` run from inside a linked worktree does NOT resolve to that worktree — hooks live in the shared common dir, so it resolves to `/…/rebar/.git/hooks/commit-msg`. The curl therefore OVERWRITES the pre-commit wrapper in the main checkout.

## Why the damage is worse than one broken worktree

`.pre-commit-config.yaml:16-19` documents the intended arrangement explicitly: pre-commit installs in MIGRATION mode, preserving Gerrit's hook as `commit-msg.legacy` and running BOTH, and warns "never install with `-f`/`--overwrite`, which would drop the Change-Id stamp and break every push to Gerrit." The curl achieves exactly that forbidden state by a different route — it replaces the wrapper rather than chaining to it, so the pre-commit `commit-msg` gate (the 50/72 message rule) stops running, and once someone later reinstalls pre-commit over it the Gerrit stamper is the half that disappears.

Either way the failure is SILENT at commit time and only surfaces at `git push gerrit`, potentially many commits later, in a DIFFERENT worktree than the one that ran the curl.

## Evidence: this is not hypothetical, it happened twice in one session

Two independent agents, working different tickets in different worktrees, each ran the documented command and each clobbered `/Users/joeoakhart/rebar/.git/hooks/commit-msg`. Both noticed and repaired it with `make hooks`, and the repaired state was verified both times:

    commit-msg          641 bytes   pre-commit wrapper
    commit-msg.legacy  3127 bytes   Gerrit stamper, contains the Change-Id logic

They noticed because they were told to report side effects. An agent not told to look would have left the repo with Change-Id stamping broken for every worktree on the host.

## Approach

Make the documented command worktree-correct and non-destructive. Options to weigh, not yet decided:

- Resolve the shared hooks dir deliberately and refuse to overwrite a pre-commit wrapper, instructing
  the user to run `make hooks` instead.
- Fold the Gerrit hook install into `make hooks` so there is ONE documented way to get both hooks and
  it is idempotent — this is the likely right answer, since `make hooks` already owns the chained
  arrangement.
- Have the command write `commit-msg.legacy` directly when a pre-commit wrapper is present.

Whichever is chosen, the docs in AGENTS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md must stop telling contributors to curl over `--git-path hooks/commit-msg`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] Running the documented install from inside a linked worktree leaves BOTH hooks functional: the
      pre-commit wrapper and the Gerrit Change-Id stamper.
- [x] A test or scripted check asserts that after the documented install, a commit made in a worktree
      receives a `Change-Id` AND is subject to the pre-commit `commit-msg` gate.
- [x] AGENTS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md no longer instruct a bare curl over
      `$(git rev-parse --git-path hooks/commit-msg)`.
- [x] The failure mode is made loud rather than silent: attempting the unsafe overwrite warns or
      refuses instead of succeeding quietly.
- [x] make lint and make typecheck pass by exit code; the default selection is green.
baseline.summary: The documented commit-msg hook install is worktree-unsafe and silently clobbers Change-Id stamping for every worktree

baseline.description:
## Problem
The close path (`rebar transition <id> in_progress closed`) acquires the ONE tickets write lock (.ticket-write.lock + .ticket-write.lock.d) and holds it across the LLM completion verifier — a multi-minute agentic operation (observed 15+ min).

## Evidence (2026-08-12, this host)
- pid 61327 `rebar transition repressive-delectable-swan in_progress closed` held /Users/joeoakhart/rebar/.tickets-tracker/.ticket-write.lock.d from 20:35:52 for 15+ minutes (holder alive and healthy the whole time; stamp: rebar-lock v2 host=name-Joes-MacBook-Pro.local pid=61327).
- A concurrent session reported it could not close a ticket due to 'long-lasting locks on the tickets branch' during exactly this window.
- Earlier this session: an implementer lost 3 plan-review runs to flock contention from sibling agents; the lock-retry work (REBAR_LOCK_RETRIES, change cc69cc1179) treats the symptom (acquire timeouts) not the cause (verifier-length holds).

## Root-cause direction (operator-specified)
The close operation should NOT hold the write lock during the LLM completion verifier. Restructure to: run the verification BEFORE acquiring the write lock, then acquire, re-check the cheap invariants (status unchanged, attestation/current-material still valid — optimistic concurrency already exists on status), append the transition event, release. The lock should bracket only the store mutation, not the LLM phase.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The write lock is not held during any LLM call on the close path (verify with a test that asserts lock-dir absence while the verifier stub runs, or equivalent instrumentation).
- [ ] Optimistic re-check under the lock prevents TOCTOU: a status/material change between verify and append fails the close with exit 10 (ConcurrencyError semantics), not a silent stale write.
- [ ] Existing close-gate semantics unchanged: signature recording, --ref retargeting, force_close_reason, and the completion precheck behave identically.
- [ ] Concurrent-close regression test: two closes on different tickets do not serialize on the LLM phase.
baseline.summary: transition close holds the tickets write lock for the whole LLM completion verification

baseline.description:
## Context

Fills the **T2 semantic-resolution tier** deferred out of the code-grounding v1 floor (epic
`8f6c-6008-33f3-4f82`, closed). v1 shipped the deterministic, polyglot, fail-open **T0
(manifest/registry existence) + T1 (ctags/tree-sitter syntactic)** floor plus a **T2
abstain-by-default seam**: `TIER_T2` exists in the closed tier vocabulary but is never emitted, and
member/dotted references abstain inline in `resolve.refute_absence` (tagged "member binding is T2").
This epic wires a real, self-contained, opt-in T2 backend behind that seam **without changing the
three-valued evidence contract (`refuted` / `match` / `abstain`) or its consumers**.

Constraints any T2 backend must respect (why T2 was deferred):
- **Not deterministic by nature.** Semantic resolution is a function of machine state (installed deps,
  build state, runtime versions), not just the artifact. Every failure mode
  (not-installed / not-built / wrong-version / hung) is indistinguishable from a genuinely fake symbol.
- **Confirm-only verdict asymmetry.** A T2 `refuted` (an asserted absence disproved — the reference
  resolves) is trustworthy; an asserted absence is suspect unless the environment is known-good. So
  T2 emits a trustworthy `refuted` and otherwise **`abstain`s** (the canonical outcome for
  "unknown") — it never sits on a deterministic blocking path.
- **Cannot be borrowed from the ambient environment.** No reliance on an externally-configured MCP
  server (e.g. Serena) or a host toolchain; the backend is self-contained + opt-in.

> **Terminology (locked to the code vocabulary).** The three-valued outcome is
> `OUTCOME_REFUTED="refuted"` / `OUTCOME_MATCH="match"` / `OUTCOME_ABSTAIN="abstain"` (`evidence.py`).
> "present" is the informal gloss for `refuted` (absence disproved); "unknown" is the informal gloss
> for `abstain`. This epic writes `refuted` / `abstain` everywhere; the glosses appear only in prose.

## Decided v1 design

**Selected v1 backend: one-shot compiler/checker-CLI diagnostics** (candidate 2), starting with
`pyright --outputjson` for Python. Rationale over the alternatives: no long-lived server (simplest to
fail-open + batch), no ambient dependency (the checker is an opt-in extra / PATH probe), and it yields
a trustworthy `refuted` when the checker runs cleanly. The **bundled LSP-client library** (candidate
1) and **containerized/hermetic** (candidate 3) tiers are **deferred** — the LSP path multiplies the
per-language server/runtime/config surface; the containerized path's gating cost is an egress-locked
single-tenant microVM sandbox (arbitrary-code-execution on untrusted client repos). Both remain future
backends behind the same seam this epic establishes.

## Design specifics (resolving the plan-review indeterminates)

**The seam is a dispatch function, not a plugin registry (Rule-of-Three).** With one concrete backend
shipping, a general `T2Backend` Protocol + registry is speculative abstraction. S2 instead adds one
module `src/rebar/grounding/semantic.py` exposing:

```python
def refute_semantic(reference, *, repo_root, config, timeout=None) -> dict | None
def available_backends() -> list[dict]   # [{name, available, version}] for grounding_info, fail-open
T2_BACKENDS: tuple[str, ...] = ("pyright",)   # the closed set of selectable backend names
```

`refute_semantic` returns a **normalized T2 evidence record** (`refuted@T2` or `abstain@T2`) or
**`None`** meaning "T2 declined to run — fall back to the caller's T1 record" (default-off path). A
future backend adds a name to `T2_BACKENDS` and a branch in `refute_semantic` — no premature Protocol.

**Escalation call-site (single owner): `oracle.refute_absence`.** After the T1/deps lanes return,
if the record is an `abstain` on a `member`/dotted reference or a not-found bare `symbol`/`import`,
`oracle.refute_absence` calls `semantic.refute_semantic(...)`; a returned `refuted@T2` replaces the
T1 abstain, otherwise the T1 record is returned unchanged. `resolve.refute_absence` (the standalone
T1 lane) is **not** modified — keeping T2 out of the T1 lane preserves T1's determinism.

**Config schema** (`.rebar/grounding.toml`, `[grounding]`, read by `resolve.load_config`; default-off):
- `t2_enabled` : bool, default `false` — the master opt-in.
- `t2_backend` : string in `T2_BACKENDS`, default `"pyright"` — an unknown value fails open to
  disabled (abstain), never a raise.
- `t2_timeout_seconds` : number, default `30` — the bounded per-invocation subprocess timeout.

**`grounding_info` change is explicit code, not free.** `oracle._backend_availability()` is a
hardcoded list today; S2 appends `*semantic.available_backends()` to it. The `grounding_info` schema's
`backends[]` name field is an open string, so a new backend name validates without a schema change
(S2 adds a conformance assertion proving this).

**pyright invocation model (the trustworthiness crux).** pyright is invoked **over the project root**
(not single-file) via the fail-open `harness.run_tool` with `t2_timeout_seconds`, so cross-module
imports resolve. The confirm-only decision for a reference in file F:
- **`refuted@T2`** iff: pyright ran and produced parseable JSON, **AND** F has **zero**
  import-resolution diagnostics (`reportMissingImports` / `reportMissingModuleSource` — the
  "environment built" precondition), **AND** there is **no** diagnostic at the reference's
  span/name (`reportAttributeAccessIssue` / `reportUndefinedVariable` / unresolved-import).
- **`abstain@T2`** (closed reason) in every other case: tool absent (`no_tool`), non-Python
  reference (`unsupported_lang`), no locatable file (`ambiguous`), unparseable output
  (`parse_error`), timeout (`timeout`), crash (`other`), F has unresolved imports so the env is
  not-built (`other`, detail records it), or a diagnostic sits at the reference (`other` — a
  suspected-absent is never asserted). One pyright run per review is cached by project root and
  reused across references (no per-reference re-invocation).

If real pyright output does not cleanly partition these diagnostic codes, the backend **abstains**
(fail-safe): S3's tests pin the mapping against captured real `--outputjson` fixtures, and any
unmapped/ambiguous code routes to `abstain`, never `refuted`.

## Related: IaC grounding lane — split out

The Terraform `validate`/Registry/`plan` tiering is a distinct domain (not a code-build environment)
— it becomes its **own sibling epic** (created by S1, linked `relates_to`), not a child here.

## Decomposition (3 stacked children, bottom → top; landed as one Gerrit feature branch)

- **S1 — ADR + IaC split (design/doc):** an ADR under `docs/adr/` recording the backend selection,
  the confirm-only mapping, the minimal-seam (no-registry) decision, and the deferral of
  LSP-lib/containerized; plus creation of the sibling IaC epic.
- **S2 — T2 seam (default-off):** `semantic.py` (`refute_semantic` / `available_backends` /
  `T2_BACKENDS`), the three config keys, escalation in `oracle.refute_absence`, and
  `_backend_availability()` reporting — all default-off so behavior is byte-identical when
  `t2_enabled=false`, proven by a regression test.
- **S3 — pyright diagnostics backend:** the Python backend `refute_semantic` dispatches to, the
  optional `grounding-t2` extra, docs (`docs/grounding.md` T2 section + config keys), and a
  per-backend fail-open matrix pinned against real pyright `--outputjson` fixtures.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] S1 lands an ADR under `docs/adr/` that names the v1 backend (pyright compiler-CLI diagnostics),
      records the confirm-only mapping and the minimal-seam decision, and creates + links a sibling
      IaC epic; the LSP-lib and containerized tiers are recorded as deferred with their tradeoffs.
- [ ] S2 lands `semantic.refute_semantic`/`available_backends`/`T2_BACKENDS`, the three
      `.rebar/grounding.toml` keys, the `oracle.refute_absence` escalation, and the
      `_backend_availability()` reporting — with `t2_enabled=false` producing byte-identical evidence
      to pre-epic behavior, proven by a default-off regression test in `tests/unit/grounding/`.
- [ ] S3 lands the pyright backend that emits `refuted@T2` when pyright runs, the file has zero
      import-resolution diagnostics, and there is no diagnostic at the reference; and emits
      `abstain@T2` with a closed reason for tool-absent / non-Python / no-file / parse-error /
      timeout / crash / env-not-built / diagnostic-at-reference.
- [ ] No code path emits an asserted absence: verified by a test asserting `refute_semantic` returns
      only `refuted` or `abstain` outcomes across the fail-open matrix.
- [ ] Self-contained + opt-in: the backend is gated behind the `grounding-t2` optional extra plus
      `t2_enabled`, and returns `abstain(no_tool)` (never a raise) when pyright is absent — proven by
      a test that runs with pyright off `PATH`.
- [ ] Fail-open matrix passes for the pyright backend (unsupported lang / no tool / no locatable file
      / crash / timeout / diagnostic-present / env-not-built → `abstain`), pinned against captured
      real `pyright --outputjson` fixtures.
- [ ] `grounding_info` (CLI `grounding-info`, MCP `grounding_info`, library `rebar.grounding_info()`)
      lists the pyright T2 backend with its detected availability/version, and the output still
      validates against `grounding_info.schema.json`.
- [ ] Proving command green: `pytest tests/unit/grounding/ && make lint` passes; all three children
      (S1–S3) closed and landed on `main` via the Gerrit feature branch.
- [ ] One self-contained, opt-in T2 backend (pyright) implements the v1 seam and emits `TIER_T2` evidence
- [ ] Every T2 outcome is `refuted` (trustworthy) or `abstain` (a closed structured reason); no code path
- [ ] With `t2_enabled=false` (the default) the full grounding test suite is byte-identical to pre-epic

## Planned file impact

- `docs/adr/00NN-code-grounding-t2-semantic-resolution.md` (S1, new ADR)
- `src/rebar/grounding/semantic.py` (S2, new T2 dispatch seam)
- `src/rebar/grounding/resolve.py` (S2, `GroundingConfig` + `load_config` T2 keys)
- `src/rebar/grounding/oracle.py` (S2, escalation + `_backend_availability`)
- `src/rebar/grounding/pyright_backend.py` (S3, the pyright backend)
- `pyproject.toml` (S3, `grounding-t2` optional extra)
- `docs/grounding.md` (S3, T2 section + config keys)
- `tests/unit/grounding/` (S2 regression + S3 fail-open matrix)
baseline.summary: Code-grounding T2: self-contained semantic-resolution backends behind the abstain-by-default seam (LSP-lib / compiler-CLI / containerized)

Discovered by the sibling sweep while fixing 12e4 (a stalled snapshot fetch burned the full 300s `_GIT_TIMEOUT`).

12e4 fixed the snapshot path: `_snapshot/git_fetch.fetch_origin` and `repo_snapshot._ensure_blobs_present` now pass `http.lowSpeedLimit`/`http.lowSpeedTime`, so a byte-starved transfer aborts on throughput in ~10s instead of at the wall-clock ceiling.

Three other NETWORK git calls still carry a 300s wall-clock bound and no low-speed abort, so each has the identical exposure:

- `src/rebar/review_bot/gerrit_client.py:367` (and the fetch at :401) — the review bot's own fetch of the Gerrit change, `_GIT_TIMEOUT = 300`. Closest sibling: same process, same per-review budget.
- `src/rebar/opcert_service/workspace.py:107,124` — `fetch --quiet review|tickets`, `_GIT_TIMEOUT = 300`.
- `src/rebar/_commands/init.py:398,419` — `_FETCH_TIMEOUT = 300`.

Deliberately NOT in scope for 12e4: they are a different remote (self-hosted Gerrit) or a different command path, no stall has been measured on them, and folding them in would have widened an already-large change that was forced to split a module. The 30s callers (`_store/push.py`, `_store/sync.py`, `_store/event_append.py`, `_ref_lock.py`) are low value — 30s is already an order of magnitude tighter than the observed stall.

Reuse the seam 12e4 built: `rebar._snapshot.git_fetch.stall_abort_args()` and `is_stall_abort()` are module-public and take no snapshot-specific state, so each call site is a splice of `*stall_abort_args()` before the subcommand plus a decision about whether to retry.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] Each of the three 300s network fetch sites passes the low-speed options.
- [x] A test per site proves a zero-byte remote aborts as a stall, and that a dribbling remote is not aborted.
- [x] No new duplicate of the abort logic: the sites reuse `git_fetch.stall_abort_args()`.
baseline.summary: Arm the throughput-keyed stall abort on the remaining 300s git fetches

`docs/adr/0004:43-48` asserts the snapshot-entry shape "has a single source of truth... Both the fetcher's output and the differs' expectations target it. When a new field is added to the snapshot, update the schema first." Nothing enforces that.

`_engine/rebar_reconciler/_snapshot_schema.py` (228 LOC) is imported by NO production module; the intended producer `fetcher.py` never imports it. The originating story declared `fetcher.py (producer validates vs schema)` as file impact; that wiring never landed.

The schema encodes a `parent` present-vs-absent distinction that gates an inbound CLEAR — a data-destroying path whose own history contains a revert titled "Revert the inbound parent clear: it destroys data."

Refined during approval: rather than a bespoke contract test, move the contract into `src/rebar/schemas/` where ~90 sibling schemas already live, loaded via `schemas.load()` and validated with `jsonschema` on a `Draft202012Validator`, with a generated TypedDict layer under a CI drift gate (`python -m rebar.schemas.gen_types`, `_build-and-test.yml:545`). The snapshot contract is the odd one out — a hand-rolled Python module outside that machinery, which is *why* nothing enforces it while 90 siblings are enforced automatically.

Real fetcher output exists for fixtures: `bridge_state/snapshots/` holds 548 files spanning 2026-06-11..06-29 with fully-populated entries. It is gitignored and contains PII (`emailAddress`, `displayName`, `accountId`), so a small redacted fixture must be derived into the tracked `tests/fixtures/jira/`, covering all three observed shapes: populated, `parent`-absent, and horizon-trimmed-empty.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] The snapshot-entry contract lives in `src/rebar/schemas/` and is loadable via `schemas.load()`
- [x] It is covered by the existing generated-types drift gate rather than a one-off check
- [x] A redacted fixture in `tests/fixtures/jira/` covers populated, `parent`-absent, and empty shapes
- [x] A fetcher field change that diverges from the contract fails CI
- [x] ADR 0004 describes the enforcement that actually exists
baseline.summary: Enforce the snapshot-entry contract through the schemas drift gate

baseline.description:
## Experiment: harness-parity oracle for completion verification (PoC, throwaway)
Operator hypothesis: completion verification is conceptually simple and works exceptionally well as a plain subagent in an agent harness with free tools; the unreliability (false rejections, insufficiency loops) lives in OUR in-process scaffolding (step budget, structured tool surface, mid-loop output contract), not in the task. This PoC measures that directly: same corpus, production verifier vs a minimal harness agent.

## Arms
- **Arm A (control): production in-process verifier** — `verify-completion` runs on the corpus tickets with the SAME harness seams the filter experiment (fabulous-lowborn-guanaco) proved: isolated per-run verdict-cache namespaces (monkeypatch `cache_dir`, completion_verdict_cache.py:59), `source='local'`/signable=false, run from a throwaway worktree's git-ignored `.expscratch/`. WHERE the guanaco control arm's transcripts are reusable (same ticket, same tree/ref, per-AC verdicts recorded), REUSE them as Arm A data instead of paying for new runs; rerun only for pairing gaps.
- **Arm B (treatment): minimal harness agent** — for each corpus ticket, a FRESH local harness subagent (Copilot CLI task agent; free, non-Bedrock) receives ONLY: the ticket's AC list verbatim, the worktree path at the pinned ref, and the instruction to verify each AC and emit JSON `{ac, verdict: PASS|FAIL|INSUFFICIENT, citations[], reason}` with file:line evidence — INSUFFICIENT is the mandatory abstain state for an AC whose evidence is not reachable with repository tools (e.g. an external-system or runtime-outcome claim); the agent must never coerce such an AC to PASS or FAIL. No rebar tooling, no step budget, no structured tool surface — plain grep/read/test-run freedom. One subagent per ticket per rep (not per AC — per-criterion fan-out was already implemented, measured, and removed for exploding cost per ticket 12b7's FORCE_CLOSE record; this experiment must not resurrect it).

## Corpus
Reuse the guanaco corpus verbatim for cross-experiment comparability: 45c1 (bettong, task, 6 ACs), 3388 (shrew, story, 10 ACs), 0e68 (wildebeast, epic, 7 ACs + 14 children), each with its in-harness adversarial variant (5 planted-unmet ACs citing symbols proven absent at ref). Ground truth: real variants = all-PASS; adversarial planted ACs = FAIL. Known Arm-A noise: guanaco observed 2 agentic false-FAILs in one epic run and 35↔55 step variance.

## Arm A rejection mapping (per AC)
Arm A per-AC outcomes come from the verifier's reconciled structured result: an AC counts as a REJECTION iff its final verdict is unmet. Among unmet ACs, classify insufficiency by the framework-derived `evidence_sufficient: false` marker (completion_reconcile.py:198-210 — model-minted markers are stripped, so this is trustworthy), the same predicate `_insufficiency_only` reuses (completion_reconcile.py:115). Report Arm A false-FAILs (unmet, evidence deemed sufficient) and evidence-insufficient unmets separately; BOTH count toward Arm A's rejection total in the decision rule.

## Arm B output validation & fallback
After each Arm B run: assert the emitted JSON parses and contains EXACTLY one entry per AC, matched by verbatim AC id/text. On parse failure or missing ACs, retry the subagent once with the same frozen prompt. If still malformed/incomplete: record every missing AC as INSUFFICIENT flagged `harness_error` (counted as rejections for the decision rule — harness fragility is a legitimate strike against Arm B, and this fail-closed rule mirrors production's per-criterion coverage check, completion_criteria.py:162). A crashed/hung subagent (no output) = one rerun; if it crashes again the rep is recorded FAILED (excluded from wall-time medians, included in the report). Validation outcomes (clean / retried / harness_error / failed-rep counts) are part of the metrics table.

## Metrics (per arm, per ticket, per rep)
False-PASS count (critical, per planted AC; an INSUFFICIENT on a planted AC is NOT a false-PASS); rejection count on real ACs = false-FAIL + INSUFFICIENT (both block a close in production, so both count toward the pain-point metric, reported separately); per-AC agreement with ground truth; wall time; Arm A Bedrock spend (tokens + $); Arm B local-harness turn/tool-call counts (cost qualitative — local harness is free per operator).

## Budget & reps
Bedrock cap **$20 total** (operator-approved) for Arm A reruns — track cumulative spend per run and STOP dispatching Arm A runs at the cap (reuse + partial pairing is an acceptable degraded result; report what was covered). Arm B is uncapped in dollars (local harness free) but capped at 2 reps/ticket-variant. Target: 2 reps per ticket-variant per arm; degrade to 1 rep on the epic if spend requires.

## Predeclared decision rule
**GO** (pursue an external-harness verifier seam in production design, feeding viral-peppy-lowchen) iff, aggregated over the corpus: (i) Arm B false-PASS = 0, AND (ii) Arm B total rejections on real ACs (false-FAIL + INSUFFICIENT) strictly < Arm A total rejections on real ACs (its false-FAILs + evidence-insufficient verdicts), AND (iii) Arm B median wall time ≤ 2× Arm A. Anything else = NO-GO or INDETERMINATE (state which and why). Apply verbatim; no post-hoc rule edits.

## Non-goals
Production integration (design goes to lowchen); per-AC fan-out (12b7); prompt engineering beyond the fixed minimal Arm-B instruction (one prompt, frozen before the first run, included in the report); closing this ticket (left in_progress for operator review).

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] Arm B prompt frozen and recorded on this ticket BEFORE the first Arm B run.
- [x] All 6 corpus ticket-variants exercised in both arms (reuse counted for Arm A), ≥1 rep each, with per-AC verdict tables.
- [x] Metrics table posted as a comment on this ticket AND on viral-peppy-lowchen: false-PASS/false-FAIL per arm, agreement, wall time, Arm A spend vs the $20 cap.
- [x] Predeclared GO/NO-GO rule applied verbatim with the arithmetic shown.
- [x] Zero Gerrit pushes; all runs source=local; harness confined to a git-ignored `.expscratch/`; Bedrock spend ≤ $20 documented.
baseline.summary: Experiment: harness-parity oracle — production verifier vs minimal free-tool harness agent (PoC)

## What
`rebar review-code` assembles its diff with a TWO-dot range `git diff base..head` (`src/rebar/llm/code_review/assemble.py`). When `head` is behind `base` (reviewing a PR branch not caught up to `origin/main`), a two-dot diff shows `head` relative to base's CURRENT tip, so every commit merged into `base` since the branch point appears as a spurious deletion. This inflates the review with a revert of unrelated work and produces phantom-deletion findings that cite real line numbers but describe changes the PR never made. Reported upstream from a client project: a 7-file PR reviewed as 11 files with ~720 phantom deletions; 3 of 5 findings were artifacts.

## Approach
Switch both diff invocations in `assemble_diff_context` from `base..head` to the THREE-dot `base...head` (merge-base) form, matching git's own PR-review convention. Three-dot diffs `head` against the merge-base of base and head, excluding unrelated commits on `base` after the branch point. The change is limited to the `diff_text is None` git path; the supplied-`diff_text` offline seam is unaffected.

## Scope / files
- `src/rebar/llm/code_review/assemble.py` — two `_git` diff calls (`diff` and `diff --name-only`).
- `tests/unit/test_code_review_assemble.py` — new behavioral regression test.

## Acceptance criteria
- A branch behind its base reviews ONLY the branch's own changed files; commits merged into base
  after the branch point are not surfaced as deletions.
- New regression test `test_diff_is_merge_base_three_dot_not_two_dot` builds a real repo with a
  branch behind main and asserts `changed_files == ["feat.py"]` (no phantom `other.py`); it fails
  under two-dot and passes under three-dot.
- lint, typecheck, and the assemble test module stay green.

## Out of scope
Run-to-run non-determinism and the supply-chain/severity findings from the same upstream report are tracked separately.
baseline.summary: code-review --base uses two-dot diff; reviewing a branch behind base surfaces phantom deletions

## Context / Problem
Running `uv` in this checkout generates a `uv.lock` at the repo root that shows up as an untracked file. rebar deliberately keeps core dependencies unpinned (`>=`), and `.github/dependabot.yml` states a `uv` ecosystem block should be added only "if a uv.lock is ever committed" — so the lockfile is a per-developer artifact that must not be tracked.

## Approach
Add a `uv.lock` entry to `.gitignore` with an explanatory comment matching the file's existing commented style, placed alongside the other per-developer tooling ignore rules (e.g. `.serena/`, `.tokensave/`). No dependency-manifest change — core deps stay unpinned `>=` by design; this only stops an already-uncommitted artifact from appearing as untracked.

## Scope
- `.gitignore` — add a commented `uv.lock` ignore rule.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `.gitignore` contains a `uv.lock` rule; verified by `git check-ignore uv.lock` printing `uv.lock` and exiting 0.
- [ ] A stray root `uv.lock` no longer appears in `git status --porcelain`.
- [ ] No other tracked files change; verified by `git diff --stat` on the change showing only `.gitignore`.
baseline.summary: Ignore per-developer uv.lock in .gitignore

baseline.description:
## The defect

The close precheck requires EVERY `- [ ]` acceptance criterion to be ticked before a ticket can close. It has no way to record that a criterion is NOT APPLICABLE.

This breaks on any ticket whose ACs are branch-exclusive — the common "decide X, then: if A do this / if B do that" shape, where satisfying one branch necessarily means the other is never performed.

## Confirmed instance 2026-08-05

Bug `a573-00ea-2bf6-4eb1` asked for an operator decision (honor the inert `CodeHealthConfig.enabled` field, or remove it) and carried both outcomes as ACs:

    - [ ] If HONORED: structural metric evaluation is gated on it, with a test proving ...
    - [ ] If REMOVED: the field, its coercion row and its config-surface entries go ...

The operator chose REMOVE. The implementing agent therefore could not satisfy the HONORED branch — by construction, not by omission. The close gate refused the close until that box was ticked, so the agent ticked a criterion describing work it had deliberately not done, and posted a comment stating the tick means N/A rather than done. It did NOT use `--force-close`, which was the right call.

Ticket authorship is a contributing cause and worth saying plainly: whoever writes a decide-then-branch ticket creates this trap. But the gate offering no expression for N/A is what converts an awkward ticket into a false record.

## Why this is worth fixing rather than tolerating

A ticked AC is load-bearing evidence in this system. The close gate reads it, the completion verifier reasons over it, and reviewers treat it as an assertion that the work was done. Once agents learn that ticking can mean "not applicable", the signal degrades for every ticket, not just branch-exclusive ones — and the degradation is invisible, because a ticked box looks identical either way.

The `[operator-attested]` tag already establishes the precedent that a criterion can be satisfied by something other than in-repo work. This is the same shape: a criterion that is legitimately not code-verifiable, for a different reason.

## Candidate approaches (weigh; not prescribed)

1. An explicit marker, e.g. `- [x] [n/a: <reason>]` or `- [~]`, that the precheck accepts and
   that records WHY. Mirrors `[operator-attested]`, so the vocabulary stays consistent.
2. Structured branch groups, so ACs can be declared mutually exclusive and the gate requires
   exactly one branch satisfied.
3. Author-side only: forbid branch-exclusive ACs and require the decision to be made before the
   ACs are written. Cheapest, but relies on discipline and does not help tickets already filed.

Option 3 alone is insufficient — the decide-then-branch shape is genuinely useful when a ticket is filed before the operator has ruled, which is exactly how a573 and dce2 were written.

## Acceptance Criteria (rescoped 2026-08-07 to the refined ruling)

N/A eligibility keys off the CLOSE DISPOSITION, not off the individual criterion. A ticket claiming COMPLETION keeps today's strict behaviour; a ticket closing as a terminal disposition (won't-fix, obsolete, not-a-bug, duplicate) has no applicable AC scan.

- [ ] The set of close classes that make the AC scan INAPPLICABLE is decided and named explicitly.
      `--class` already exists on bug closes (regression, plan_defect, env_integration, flaky,
      preexisting, not_a_bug, duplicate, escalated, undetermined); state which of these are terminal
      dispositions, and whether a won't-fix / obsolete class needs adding — 3b92 had no honest class
      to use and was force-closed as a result
- [ ] Closing under a terminal-disposition class does NOT run the unchecked-AC precheck, and records
      the class as the reason the criteria were not evaluated
- [ ] Closing as COMPLETED is UNCHANGED: an unmet criterion still fails the close, and the remedy is
      still to remediate the criterion. A test pins that this path did not weaken
- [ ] A test proves a terminal-disposition close succeeds with unchecked criteria present AND that the
      same ticket closing as completed still fails
- [ ] `--force-close` is no longer the routine answer for an obsolete ticket; the CLI message on a
      failed close points at the class mechanism rather than straight at the override (this is the
      steering defect 218e reports separately)
- [ ] Non-bug types (task, story, epic) are covered too, or their exclusion is stated with a reason —
      3b92, 5dd2, e5ec, 39c5 and 83f2 were all tasks, and all were force-closed
- [ ] The distinction is documented where AC authors will see it, alongside `[operator-attested]`

## Out of scope

A PER-CRITERION N/A marker. That was the original request and it is rejected: on a ticket claiming completion, a criterion nobody can satisfy means the plan was written wrong, and letting an author mark it N/A converts that signal into a checkbox. The disposition-level mechanism above solves the genuine case without opening that door.
baseline.summary: The close gate cannot express an N/A acceptance criterion, so mutually-exclusive ACs force a false tick

# S5 — Trusted-proxy passthrough verifier

## Why
Many organizations terminate authentication at an edge proxy / gateway (oauth2-proxy, API Gateway, ALB) and want the backend to trust the already-authenticated identity — and it is the only in-scope path for identity systems that are not token issuers (e.g. GitHub-user via oauth2-proxy). This verifier lets rebar delegate auth to that fronting proxy safely, through the SAME composite contract as token verifiers.

## What
Add a **trusted-proxy** mode to `src/rebar/_mcp_auth.py`, activated by including `proxy` in the `mcp.auth_strategies` list (the strategy-selection config key **introduced by S2**, this story's dependency — not a pre-existing seam), with flat config keys it registers: `auth_proxy_secret_env` (NAME of an env var holding the proxy shared secret — no plaintext secret in config), `auth_proxy_secret_header` (default `x-proxy-auth`), `auth_proxy_identity_header` (default `x-forwarded-user`), and `auth_proxy_scopes` (comma-separated fixed scope set granted to proxy-authenticated principals; OPTIONAL, defaults to an EMPTY set — a proxy-authenticated principal then holds no scopes and is denied 403 by any non-empty `auth_required_scopes` until scopes are configured). It comprises a small ASGI middleware plus a `TokenVerifier`-shaped component so that proxy identity flows through the **same composite**, not around it:
- The **middleware** runs before the MCP app: it validates the shared-secret header (constant-time)
  and, only if valid, extracts the identity header into a request-scoped principal; otherwise it
  strips it. It **strips the entire `X-Forwarded-*` family** (and the configured identity/secret
  headers) from any inbound request that does not present the valid secret, normalizing header-name
  case and underscore/dash variants to defeat smuggling.
- The **verifier** turns that verified request-scoped identity into an `AccessToken` with
  `client_id`=the identity, `scopes`=`auth_proxy_scopes`, and **`resource=auth_resource_server_url`**
  so it passes the composite audience check exactly like a token verifier. If no verified proxy
  identity is present it returns None (composite falls through / denies) — it never accepts on a
  missing/invalid secret.
- **Ordering:** the proxy verifier participates in the composite `auth_strategies` order like any
  other; a bare request with no valid proxy identity is not accepted by it, so a co-configured bearer
  verifier still gets its turn. Adds the `auth_proxy_*` fields to `McpConfig`/`_SECTIONS['mcp']` (`src/rebar/_config_schema.py`); their derived `REBAR_MCP_AUTH_PROXY_*` env-var names go in `MCP_ENV_VARS` (`src/rebar/mcp_server.py`) + `server.json`; `scripts/check_server_manifest.py` passes (docs regenerated by S7).

## Approach & rationale
Implement the oauth2-proxy-blessed trusted-header pattern, and route the result through the composite (not around it) so the single audience/fail-closed choke point (S2) still applies. Bind HTTP to loopback (S1 default) so only the proxy can reach the server; require a proxy shared secret; strip any inbound identity/forwarded headers unless the secret is valid. This is the documented mitigation for the forwarded-header-spoofing class (oauth2-proxy CVE-2026-40575 / CVE-2025-64484). A tiny ASGI middleware is the right seam because forwarded identity lives on headers the token-only `verify_token` seam does not see.

## Scope
The trusted-proxy verifier + its header-guard middleware only, on the S2 seam. Subset of the epic. Depends on S2. Independent of S3/S4/S6.

## Security
Boundary-crossing and itself a spoofing surface. Hard requirements:
- **Loopback bind** is the intended deployment (S1 default); a non-loopback bind is governed by S1's
  existing non-loopback gate (both allowlists + TLS-at-edge ack) — no new bind key.
- **Operator prerequisite (documented, loud):** the fronting proxy MUST overwrite/strip all
  client-supplied identity and forwarded headers before adding its own; rebar additionally strips the
  entire `X-Forwarded-*` family on its side unless the shared secret validates.
- The env var named by `auth_proxy_secret_env` MUST be present and non-empty at startup or the proxy
  verifier refuses to start (fail-closed).
- The shared secret proves "from the proxy," not identity authenticity — so identity is trusted ONLY
  when the secret validates AND the header survived rebar's strip-then-repopulate; a constant-time
  compare gates it; header-name normalization defeats underscore/case smuggling.
- The minted `AccessToken` carries `resource=auth_resource_server_url`, so it is still subject to the
  composite audience check; fail-closed (no valid secret → no identity → 401).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] The `auth_proxy_*` config fields exist in `McpConfig`/`_SECTIONS['mcp']` (`_config_schema.py`);
      their derived `REBAR_MCP_AUTH_PROXY_*` env-var names are in `MCP_ENV_VARS` (`mcp_server.py`) +
      `server.json`; and `scripts/check_server_manifest.py` passes (observable oracle: manifest drift
      test green; both files contain the new env-var names). Docs regenerated by S7.
- [ ] Unit test (tier: unit — the ASGI middleware + verifier exercised directly) asserts: with a
      valid `auth_proxy_secret` header, the identity header yields an `AccessToken` whose
      `client_id`=identity, `scopes`=`auth_proxy_scopes`, and `resource==auth_resource_server_url`;
      without the secret, the identity header is stripped and the request is unauthenticated (401).
- [ ] Unit test asserts a client cannot spoof identity: sending `x-forwarded-user` (or the
      underscore/case variants `X_Forwarded_User`, `X-FORWARDED-USER`) directly WITHOUT the valid
      secret is stripped and never trusted; and that the entire `X-Forwarded-*` family is stripped in
      that case (negative controls for each variant).
- [ ] Unit test asserts the verifier refuses to start when the env var named by `auth_proxy_secret_env`
      is absent or empty (observable oracle: startup raises a clear message).
- [ ] Unit test asserts `auth_proxy_scopes` defaults to an empty set when unset, so a valid proxy
      principal holds no scopes and is denied 403 by a non-empty `auth_required_scopes` (observable
      oracle: 403 with empty proxy scopes vs 200 once the required scope is granted).
- [ ] Integration test (httpx `ASGITransport`) asserts an authenticated proxy request (valid secret +
      identity header) → 200, and that the proxy-minted token still passes the composite audience
      check; a bare request → 401.
- [ ] Integration test asserts composition: with `auth_strategies=proxy,static`, a request with no
      proxy identity but a valid static token still succeeds (proxy verifier returns None, static
      accepts) — observable oracle: 200.
- [ ] `make lint && make typecheck && make test` pass.

## Compatibility
Additive, opt-in via the `proxy` strategy. No change to other verifiers or the stdio path.
baseline.summary: S5 — Trusted-proxy passthrough verifier

baseline.description:
The snapshot janitor never garbage-collects the new pinned ticket-store cache entries (`<store>/tickets-<sha>/`) introduced in PR #67, so they accumulate unboundedly as the `tickets` branch changes — a local-disk leak in the gate snapshot cache. They are also absent from the janitor's byte-total accounting.

## Reproduction Steps
1. Run the plan-review / completion gates repeatedly while the `tickets` branch HEAD changes between runs (normal: every ticket write advances it).
2. Each distinct tickets SHA materializes a fresh `<store>/tickets-<sha>/.tickets-tracker/` copy of the whole ticket store.
3. Inspect the snapshot store (`REBAR_GATE_TMPDIR` / `store_root()`): the `tickets-<sha>` dirs accumulate and are never evicted.

## Expected vs Actual
- Expected: the janitor evicts stale `tickets-<sha>` entries by the same grace/LRU/size policy it applies to code-snapshot `<sha>` entries, and counts them in the byte total.
- Actual: `src/rebar/_snapshot/janitor.py:_is_entry` treats an entry as `all(c in "0123456789abcdef" for c in name)` — the `tickets-` prefix is non-hex, so `_is_entry("tickets-<sha>")` is False. `_entries()` therefore excludes them: they are never evicted (leak) and never counted (under-reported cache size).

## Root Cause
`_is_entry` (janitor.py) recognizes only all-hex directory names; PR #67's `tickets-<sha>` entries don't match.

## Fix direction
Extend `_is_entry` to also recognize `tickets-<40hex>` (e.g. accept names matching `^(tickets-)?[0-9a-f]{40}$`), so `_entries()` includes them for eviction + accounting. Verify `_evict`/`_remove_sidecars` behave for a `tickets-`-named entry (no caveats sidecar — the unlink is try/except, harmless). Add a janitor test that a stale `tickets-<sha>` entry is evicted past the grace window.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `_is_entry` returns True for a `tickets-<40hex>` dir; `_entries()` includes it.
- [ ] The janitor evicts a stale `tickets-<sha>` entry (past grace) and counts it in the byte total.
- [ ] A regression test covers eviction + accounting of a `tickets-<sha>` entry.
- [ ] Code-snapshot `<sha>` entry handling is unchanged.
- [ ] Fix lands via PR to main.
baseline.summary: snapshot janitor leaks pinned ticket-store entries (tickets-<sha> not GC'd)

## Context
Pure mutation plans still need to represent binding lifecycle decisions and prerequisite ordering without performing effects. Selection, filters, mode caps, and safety limits must exclude work before intents are eligible.

## Outcome
Add versioned lifecycle intents and explicit inter-ticket dependencies to `TicketPlan`, and apply every global selection/limit before any lifecycle or remote effect.

## Plan
1. Model bind, confirm, re-key, retire, baseline, and comment-identity changes as versioned intents only.
2. Encode create-before-link and parent-before-child prerequisites. A blocked prerequisite yields deferred disposition and emits no out-of-order mutation.
3. Move selection, filter, mode cap, and global safety limit decisions into pre-effect planning.
4. Cover tombstones, pending/index lag, moved keys, impossible links, partial snapshots, and filtered passes with ticket-sourced tables.

## Testing
Pure tables assert exact intent/dependency/disposition values and poison repository/provider writes. Ordering tests vary each limit independently.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Every named binding change is represented as a versioned lifecycle intent and performs no write during planning.
- [ ] Create-before-link and parent-before-child prerequisites are explicit plan dependencies.
- [ ] Blocked prerequisites produce deferred plans and no out-of-order mutation.
- [ ] Selection, filter, mode cap, and global safety limits exclude work before any intent or remote effect is eligible.
- [ ] Ticket-sourced tombstone, index-lag, move, link, partial-snapshot, and filtered cases have deterministic dispositions.

## Out of scope
Preview output and production coordinator execution.
baseline.summary: RP-03 S2 T2 — Plan lifecycle intents, dependencies, and pre-effect limits

# restore_deleted_sources misses deletions a PATH-scoped walk would find

## Corrected diagnosis (the original filing was wrong)
This bug was filed claiming plain `git log` skips MERGE commits, so a deletion reaching HEAD through a merge was invisible. That is FALSE. Measured on the live store against ticket f130's lost EDIT (a440f6d5-6aa1-4669-9908-5fb955ad6a53, which carried that ticket's 2719-char description):

    git log --diff-filter=D -- <tid>/                          -> 0 hits
    git log --diff-filter=D --full-history -- <tid>/           -> 0 hits
    git log --diff-filter=D -m -- <tid>/                       -> 0 hits
    git log --diff-filter=D --diff-merges=first-parent -- ...  -> 0 hits
    git log --all --diff-filter=D -- <tid>/                    -> 0 hits
    git log --all --diff-filter=D        (no pathspec)         -> 0 hits
    git log --diff-filter=D -- <tid>/*<uuid>*                  -> 1 hit

Every merge-diff mode and `--all` changes nothing. ONLY narrowing the pathspec from the DIRECTORY to the FILE (or a per-uuid glob) finds it. So this is a pathspec-SCOPE effect under git's path history simplification — not merge-diff display, and not reachability. The fix the original acceptance criteria implied (add a diff-merges mode) would have shipped without fixing anything.

## Impact
`restore_deleted_sources` enumerates deletions with ONE ticket-scoped `git log --diff-filter=D --name-only -- <tid>/` pass. Anything that walk misses stays unrecoverable and the ticket keeps a SNAPSHOT_MISSING_SOURCES finding permanently. Observed on f130 during the b636 remediation; recovered by hand at the time.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] A targeted per-uuid fallback (`git log --diff-filter=D -- <tid>/*<uuid>*`) recovers
      sources the directory-scoped walk misses.
- [x] The fallback is BOUNDED to the uuids the snapshot still cites as absent after the cheap
      pass — a glob pathspec walks full history per uuid and is markedly slower (one probe
      command timed out at 10 minutes).
- [x] NEWEST-deletion-wins is preserved in the fallback (git streams newest-first, first hit
      wins), matching `_deleted_history`.
- [x] Held-out test: the fallback recovers an event when the directory-scoped walk is stubbed
      empty. Verified RED (fails with the fallback call removed) then GREEN.
- [x] Module-size: `fsck_repair` was at its 800-line cap, so the restore cluster
      (`_deleted_history`, `_deleted_path_for_uuid`, `_uuid_fallback`,
      `restore_deleted_sources`, `rebuild_with_restore`) moves to a new `fsck_restore` leaf —
      633/204 lines, both inside the 100-800 band. `fsck_repair` owns snapshot-source
      ACCOUNTING and the repair decision; `fsck_restore` owns recovering the bytes.
      `fsck_repair` re-exports the public names; `fsck_restore` imports
      `snapshot_missing_sources` lazily so the two do not form a cycle. Neither moved function
      carries a complexity-baseline entry, so the split adds none.
baseline.summary: restore_deleted_sources misses events deleted in a merge commit (git log --diff-filter=D skips merges)

# S9 — ADR + documentation for the provider seam and the two-tier support policy

## Context / Problem

After S1–S8 rebar has a provider seam, a tier policy, a Bedrock path, and tier-stamped verdicts — none of it written down. `docs/llm-framework.md:121-143` still describes provider support as "pydantic-ai resolves the provider from the model string" with no mention of tiers, Bedrock, or what a best-effort provider means for a signed verdict, and its `:131-133` local-server recipe describes behavior that only becomes true in S4. Without a recorded decision, the next Bedrock/gateway request reopens the same argument as a one-off, which is the failure mode this epic exists to end.

## Approach

Write one ADR recording the decisions and, importantly, the rejected alternatives with their evidence: the seam is pydantic-ai's `provider_factory` hook and capabilities come from `ModelProfile`; two support tiers with Anthropic and Bedrock first-class; native Bedrock rather than a gateway; LiteLLM rejected as an in-process dependency but reachable as a proxy; verdicts sign on every tier but stamp the tier. Then bring `docs/llm-framework.md` in line with what the code now does, including the Bedrock recipe, the tier table, and what tier means for an attestation consumer.

The ADR also records the two operational findings this epic turned up, so they are not rediscovered: the IMDS hop-limit constraint and its containment [rebar:9249-1569-7be9-4f67], and the measured relationship between cross-region inference profiles and prompt caching [rebar:2932-8a98-6d70-4550].

**Alternative rejected:** documenting in `docs/llm-framework.md` only. That records the *what* but not the *why*, and rebar's ADR set is where rejected alternatives live — without them the LiteLLM and gateway options get re-proposed.

## Scope

- `docs/adr/00NN-llm-provider-seam-and-support-tiers.md` (new).
- `docs/llm-framework.md` — the provider section (`:121-143`) and the env table (`:224-226`).
- `docs/env-vars.md` — regenerated.
- `README.md` — one line if the provider story is summarized there.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] the ADR exists, is `Accepted`, and names each rejected alternative (in-process LiteLLM, gateway-fronted
      Bedrock, refuse-to-sign off-tier, Bedrock API key in SSM, cross-provider fallback) with the evidence that
      rejected it
- [x] [operator-attested] every runnable command in `docs/llm-framework.md`'s provider section has been executed and produced the
      documented result, confirmed in a ticket comment
- [x] the docs state, for each tier, what is guaranteed (tests, parity) and what a consumer can infer from a
      verdict's stamped tier
- [x] [operator-attested] the documented generator produces NO diff to `docs/env-vars.md`, evidenced by the
      command and its empty-diff output quoted in a comment
baseline.summary: S9 — ADR + documentation for the provider seam and the two-tier support policy
